question: What is the principal layout difference between the pathway grade crossing and the sidewalk grade crossing in Figure 8E-1?
model_answer: Direct Answer: The principal layout difference shown in Figure 8E-1 is the relationship to the roadway. In Panel A, the pathway occupies its own independent "Pathway right-of-way" and crosses the tracks with no adjacent roadway, whereas in Panel B the sidewalk runs parallel and immediately adjacent to a roadway within the "Highway right-of-way," so both cross the tracks together. This matters because roadway grade crossing traffic control devices can typically warn sidewalk users but not pathway users. Standards (mandatory): - "Detectable warnings (see Chapter 3C) shall be used at pathway grade crossings where pedestrian travel is permitted and at sidewalk grade crossings and shall extend across the full width of the pathway or sidewalk." (Both panels of Figure 8E-1 show detectable warnings on each approach.) Visual evidence: [Image 1] Figure 8E-1 shows Panel A with a stand-alone pathway crossing the railroad within its own labeled "Pathway right-of-way," and Panel B with a sidewalk directly alongside a roadway (with yellow centerline) inside a labeled "Highway right-of-way," with detectable warnings marked on both approaches in each panel. [Image 2] The full page confirms the accompanying Support text explaining that a pathway is frequently placed in its own right-of-way independent of any roadway, while a sidewalk runs parallel to a roadway within the highway right-of-way close to the traveled way. Citations: - Section 8E.01 Support §4 (p.1035) - Section 8E.04 Standard §7 (p.1038) - Figure 8E-1 (p.1035) - Page 1076
gold_answer: The pathway crossing is on a separate pathway alignment outside the roadway, whereas the sidewalk crossing is part of the highway corridor alongside the roadway and crosses the tracks with the roadway.
